doc.title: Dick Spottswood interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 13, 2023

title: Does bluegrass swing, and where string basses came from
summary: On Ed Shaughnessy's quote, he says bluegrass can swing but is not jazz, and credits 1930s jukeboxes for string bass in western bands.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Well said. Drummer Ed Shaughnessy, I asked him once if he could define swing. And he said he thought he could but, this is a quote, he says, “Youngsters and even oldsters, they mix up the terms to swing and lock it exclusively into jazz music. Now I think bluegrass music swings like hell, without drums, it swings. It’s infectious.” Do you think bluegrass music swings like Ed does?
My problem goes back further than that. When you say “swing” are you referring to a noun or a verb?
That was Ed’s point also that I’m referring to it, the process of — a verb.

The music swings or it doesn’t swing. Bluegrass can swing but swing is not its, that’s not where the music starts from. It’s not jazz music. It’s music where basically out of the Virginia, West Virginia, Kentucky, Tennessee, that little quadrant of — a quadrant — because actually it’s five states down there in that little nexus around Bristol, Virginia where Jimmy Rodgers and the Carter family kind of — they didn’t define modern country music but they kind of set down some informal barriers as to what hillbilly music would sound like and wouldn’t sound like, and it did not sound like jazz. It doesn’t mean

that you couldn’t play according to that rhythm. When jukeboxes came around in the 1930s all of a sudden you needed string basses for more than just big dance bands. You had to have string basses so the people could dance into taverns where there were only jukeboxes and they couldn’t hear the beat unless the jukebox record had a bass on it. That’s where the basses come from according to me.

And so beginning in the early 30s the western bands like the Light Crust Doughboys and Bob Wills and Milton Brown — they all had bass players. Then up in Chicago the Barn Dance on WLS — am I getting that wrong — anyway the Saturday Night Barn Dance out of Chicago — my memory’s got huge holes in it — who had the Kentucky Ramblers and the leader was a bass player, Roy Acuff’s hit records from the mid-30s from Knoxville with Knoxville people were the ones that had a string bass in it. And I think the presence or absence of a string bass in bluegrass has a lot to do with its jazz related qualities. But I think it kind of ends with the string bass because when you hear what the guitar and the banjo and the mandolin are playing, they’re still referring back to Saturday night waltzes and mountain reels and 1-4-5 harmonies and all of the things that make great hillbilly music so precious and so different. And I think it’s useful to keep that distinction except when Bill Monroe wanted to play a blues or something and then he’d get the bass up there and Bill could sing the blues right up there with Bob Wills and Brownie McGee.
